scenes.tts: The oxygen in your next breath is, in part, made of leftovers. What it was left over from is the story. Rewind about three billion years. Watch the gauge. The air holds almost no oxygen. Something had to fill this sky. And something held it back.
scenes.caption: The oxygen in your next breath is, in part, made of leftovers. What it was left over from is the story. Rewind about 3 billion years. Watch the gauge. The air holds almost no oxygen. Something had to fill this sky. And something held it back.
scenes.visual: No title first. Open TIGHT on today's sky and keep the first five seconds simple: only two things are on screen. (1) A dark sky crowded with about 60 slowly drifting BLUE oxygen pips (plain discs, never two joined circles). (2) The GAUGE, a tall glass tube filled BLUE up to a dashed tick marked 'today', headed 'O2 in air', with the small tag 'schematic' under it from the first frame. No scrubber yet. On 'next breath': the pips drift toward the viewer and swell slightly. On 'Leftovers from what': a large '?' in TEXT white lands beside the gauge. On 'Rewind': the '?' fades; the TIME SCRUBBER draws on along the bottom edge (linear scale, right end 'today') and its playhead sweeps hard left to the left end; the readout settles at 'about 3 billion years ago'. In the same move the view pulls back to the whole WORLD (the full-frame cross-section: sky, sea, shallow shelf on the left, deep basin on the right, dark land with one cone at far left), the pips drain out of the sky and the gauge falls in one smooth ease to a thin sliver. As the world comes into view it is already alive, with no narration needed: the sea surface shimmers (a travelling sine line, it never stops again), the cone vents GREY puffs (they never stop), and a GOLD sun with three slow rays sits top left. On 'Watch the gauge': the gauge tube brightens and a white bracket closes on its thin sliver, so the eye learns where to look. On 'almost no oxygen': the sliver pulses once; three lonely pips are all that is left in the sky. On 'had to fill': a dashed ghost of the full level flashes up at the 'today' tick. On 'held it back': the ghost level sinks back down onto the sliver, and a '?' in TEXT white settles beside the empty tube and stays as the scene ends.
scenes.narration: The oxygen in your next breath is, in part, made of leftovers. What it was left over from is the story. Rewind about 3 billion years. Watch the gauge. The air holds almost no oxygen. Something had to fill this sky. And something held it back.

scenes.visual: Title card over the dimmed world (do not cut to black): HOW EARTH GOT ITS OXYGEN, with the gold rule. The surface keeps shimmering and the plume keeps drifting behind it. Two seconds, then the card lifts and the world returns to full brightness.

scenes.tts: Nobody saw this world, so we rebuild it from ancient rocks. The sea held dissolved iron. That iron had electrons to give. But with little oxygen to take them, much of that iron stayed dissolved.
scenes.visual: The whole world, playhead at 'about 3 billion years ago', gauge a sliver. The sky is plain and dark: no haze is drawn in this film. On 'ancient rocks': the seabed rock under the basin brightens for a beat with the label 'rebuilt from ancient rocks' (size 28), then the label fades; one thin, dull RED stripe already lies on the basin floor, unlabelled (some striped rock is older than this moment). On 'The sea held': about 40 GREY discs fade in through the water, densest in the deep basin, each drifting on its own slow path; the label 'dissolved iron' arrives after they have settled. Show, then tell: BEFORE 'electrons to give', the view pushes in on one disc until it fills a third of the frame and one small YELLOW dot is seen riding on its rim; on 'electrons to give' the dot glints and the label 'electron' (YELLOW, size 28) points at it for a beat. On 'little oxygen': the view widens enough to show that no blue pip is anywhere near it; the three in the sky are too few to matter. On 'stayed dissolved': pull back out; every grey disc now shows its yellow dot and keeps drifting.
scenes.narration: Nobody saw this world, so we rebuild it from ancient rocks. The sea held dissolved iron. That iron had electrons to give. But with little oxygen to take them, much of that iron stayed dissolved.

scenes.tts: Life was already here, and all of it was microbial. Many of these cells likely made energy without oxygen, by fermenting or by making methane. Remember them. They come back near the end.
scenes.visual: Same world; the view sinks so the seabed (shelf and basin floor) fills the lower two thirds of the frame. On 'already here': a carpet of small PURPLE rods and spheres fades up along the shelf and the basin floor, each wobbling in place on an updater. One label only: 'microbes' (size 28). On 'without oxygen': the view tilts up for a beat to show the empty water above them, with no blue anywhere, and comes back down. On 'fermenting': a patch of purple cells on the shelf pulses, and the cells in it split in two (they are living well). On 'making methane': a cluster on the basin floor releases small GREY rings, each carrying a yellow dot like the iron, that rise slowly and keep rising for the rest of the film; the label 'methane' rides up with the first ring and fades. No 'likely' tag: the hedge is in the voice. On 'Remember them': a thin white ring closes around one cluster of purple cells and holds. On 'come back': the ring shrinks to a small bookmark tick on that cluster, which stays on it until s14.
scenes.narration: Life was already here, and all of it was microbial. Many of these cells likely made energy without oxygen, by fermenting or by making methane. Remember them. They come back near the end.

scenes.tts: Then came a new trick. Water holds its electrons tightly. Cyanobacteria learned to pull them out, powered by sunlight. They kept the electrons to build their own food. The waste was oxygen gas, and they let it go.
scenes.visual: The playhead does not move; it turns hollow (outline only) and its readout changes to 'when? debated'. It turns solid and starts creeping again in s08. The view pushes in hard on the sunlit shelf until ONE cell fills the frame: a GREEN capsule about 6 units long with a notch (a mouth) on its upper left and a small vent on its upper right. It appears and settles on 'a new trick', before it is named. On 'Water holds': two TEAL droplets drift up to the mouth, each with two YELLOW dots held tight inside it (they jitter but cannot leave); they bump the closed mouth and bounce. On 'Cyanobacteria': the label 'cyanobacterium' lands under the cell. On 'pull them out': the mouth opens and takes both droplets in. On 'powered by sunlight': a GOLD ray strikes the capsule, the capsule flashes brighter green, and the four yellow dots are torn out of the droplets. On 'kept the electrons': the four yellow dots slide deep into the capsule and stay there, glowing. On 'own food': inside the capsule the four dots sink into a plain rounded GREEN block that grows by one notch (a plain block labelled 'food', no structure). On 'The waste': one BLUE bubble swells at the vent. On 'let it go': the bubble pops free and rises out of the top of the frame. The whole cycle (two droplets in, ray, four dots kept, the block grows, one bubble out) then repeats twice more, faster, with no new labels.
scenes.narration: Then came a new trick. Water holds its electrons tightly. Cyanobacteria learned to pull them out, powered by sunlight. They kept the electrons to build their own food. The waste was oxygen gas, and they let it go.

scenes.tts: In shallow seas, these cells spread as sticky mats. So here is a puzzle. The mats were releasing oxygen. Why did the air not fill with it right away?
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole world. On 'spread': the one green capsule multiplies sideways into a GREEN mat that carpets the shallow shelf and breathes (slow pulse on an updater); label 'cyanobacterial mats'. On 'here is a puzzle': the view frames mat, water column and gauge together. On 'releasing oxygen': streams of small BLUE bubbles leave the mat and rise (they keep streaming for the rest of the film). Each bubble fades out part-way up the water, at different heights, with no visible cause yet. On 'Why did the air': the gauge tube brightens; its sliver has not moved; the white bracket from s00 marks the unmoved level again. The question writes on above the sea in two lines, size 34: 'The mats release oxygen.' / 'Why does the air not fill?'
scenes.narration: In shallow seas, these cells spread as sticky mats. So here is a puzzle. The mats were releasing oxygen. Why did the air not fill with it right away?

scenes.visual: Hold the question. The two-line question stays. Bubbles keep leaving the mat and keep vanishing in mid-water; the grey iron discs keep drifting through the same water; the gauge sliver trembles but does not rise; the surface shimmers. Nothing new appears.

scenes.tts: Because oxygen had many other places to go. Oxygen strongly pulls in electrons. Each oxygen molecule can take four. And the sea held iron with electrons to give. So iron handed its electrons to oxygen, formed rust-like minerals, and sank.
scenes.visual: The question lifts away. On 'other places to go': the view dives into mid-water after one bubble and stops when that bubble fills a quarter of the frame. On 'strongly pulls in': the HERO BUBBLE shows what it is: a BLUE disc with four empty sockets (small dark dashed circles) around its rim, each socket tugging at the water with a faint inward pulse. On 'can take four': the four sockets light in turn, one, two, three, four, so the number is seen as it is said. On 'iron with electrons': four GREY iron discs drift in from the four corners, each with its YELLOW dot on the rim. On 'handed its electrons': one by one the four yellow dots jump from iron to socket (four small clicks, about 0.4 s apart). As each dot leaves, that iron disc turns from GREY to RED. On 'formed rust': the four red discs pull together into one RED flake (a small rough diamond) and the bubble, its sockets full, is gone: no blue is left. Label 'rust-like mineral' on the flake. On 'and sank': the flake falls out of the bottom of the frame; pull back to the whole world, where the same thing is now visibly happening everywhere: bubbles meet grey discs, flash, and red flakes drift down through the basin like slow rain. The gauge has still not moved.
scenes.narration: Because oxygen had many other places to go. Oxygen strongly pulls in electrons. Each oxygen molecule can take four. And the sea held iron with electrons to give. So iron handed its electrons to oxygen, formed rust-like minerals, and sank.

scenes.tts: Layer by layer, iron and silica built striped rock on the sea floor. These are banded iron formations, and much of the iron we mine today comes from them. Some layers may be the work of microbes that rust iron without any oxygen.
scenes.visual: The view settles on the deep basin so the basin floor and the water above it fill the frame; the gauge stays in view at the right. The playhead turns solid again and creeps right through the whole scene; its readout shows no number until the band lights in s12 (until then it reads 'before the rise'). On 'Layer by layer': falling red flakes settle onto the thin stripe already there and thicken it into a RED stripe. On 'and silica': a pale GREY stripe grows on top, with a small tag 'silica' that points at it and fades (the word gets its picture). Then red; then grey: eight stripes build upward in time with the sentence, each one a transformation of what lands on it. The stack shows before it is named; on 'banded iron formations' the label lands beside it. On 'iron we mine': a white bracket closes around the whole striped stack and a small plain pick-and-block icon in TEXT white taps it; tag 'mined today'. On 'Some layers may': bracket, icon and tag fade, and the view lifts to the dim sunlit water above the stack: a purple microbe, lit by one faint GOLD ray, takes the yellow dot from a nearby grey iron disc into itself; the disc turns red and sinks to join a red stripe, with no blue bubble anywhere near; tag 'without oxygen?' (question mark kept). Flakes keep falling throughout.
scenes.narration: Layer by layer, iron and silica built striped rock on the sea floor. These are banded iron formations, and much of the iron we mine today comes from them. Some layers may be the work of microbes that rust iron without any oxygen.

scenes.tts: Iron was not the only taker. Volcanic gases, methane, and minerals on land all consumed oxygen too. As an analogy, picture a bathtub. The mats are the tap. Every one of those takers is an open drain.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole world; the striped stack stays on the basin floor (it never leaves again). A few bubbles now get past the iron and break the surface as blue pips. On 'not the only taker': the view lifts to follow three pips into the sky. On 'Volcanic gases': a GREY plume puff, yellow dot on its rim, drifts into the first pip; the dot jumps, the pip is gone, the puff goes dull. On 'methane': a grey methane ring rising from the purple microbes does the same to the second pip. On 'minerals on land': the third pip drifts to the shore, where a row of grey rock blocks each carry a yellow dot; one block takes the pip and goes dull like the puff (only iron ever turns red). Labels appear only after each act: 'volcanic gas', 'methane', 'land minerals'. On 'As an analogy': the three labels fade and a small tag 'analogy' lands at the top of the frame. On 'are the tap': the word 'tap' (TEXT white, size 34) lands over the mat and the mat's bubble stream brightens. On 'open drain': the word 'drains' lands with four short ticks pointing at iron, plume, methane and shore, and one bubble in turn is taken at each tick (four small moves, so the picture does not sit still); the gauge tube pulses once as the tub's water level. No bathtub is drawn.
scenes.narration: Iron was not the only taker. Volcanic gases, methane, and minerals on land all consumed oxygen too. As an analogy, picture a bathtub. The mats are the tap. Every one of those takers is an open drain.

scenes.tts: Here is the idea to hold on to. Making oxygen is only half of the story. The air keeps only the oxygen that nothing else takes first.
scenes.visual: The whole world, running: the mat streams bubbles, the four takers each take theirs, red flakes fall, the stack sits on the floor. 'tap', 'drains' and 'analogy' fade on 'hold on to'. On 'only half': the mat's bubble stream brightens on its own while everything else dims slightly. On 'The air keeps': the world returns to full brightness and the view follows ONE bubble all the way: past the iron, through the surface, past the plume, up into the gauge, where the sliver ticks up by a hair. On 'takes first': the guiding line writes on across the sky in two lines, size 36, TEXT white with 'oxygen' in BLUE: 'The air keeps only the oxygen' / 'that nothing else takes first.' While it holds, a second bubble sets out on the same path and is taken by the iron half-way up, so the line is acted out under itself and the frame is never still.
scenes.narration: Here is the idea to hold on to. Making oxygen is only half of the story. The air keeps only the oxygen that nothing else takes first.

scenes.tts: So when did the tap turn on? Cyanobacteria most likely arose well before oxygen built up. By how long is debated. Some rocks hint at brief whiffs of oxygen before the lasting rise.
scenes.visual: The guiding line fades. The TIME SCRUBBER thickens and rises a little into the frame so it can be read; the world keeps running above it; the playhead keeps its slow creep to the right. On 'tap turn on': the word 'tap' flashes once more over the mat, and a GREEN span starts to draw along the scrubber from the playhead back toward the left. On 'well before': the span runs on leftward, solid near the playhead and breaking into dashes that fade out; no left end is drawn. On 'is debated': the dashed part shimmers and the tag 'start debated' lands on it. On 'brief whiffs': the gauge sliver jumps three small times and falls back each time, and each time a puff of blue pips flickers in the sky and is taken by the plume; tag 'whiffs?' beside the gauge (question mark kept). On 'lasting rise': the playhead arrives at the left edge of a still-unlit band on the scrubber and stops.
scenes.narration: So when did the tap turn on? Cyanobacteria most likely arose well before oxygen built up. By how long is debated. Some rocks hint at brief whiffs of oxygen before the lasting rise.

scenes.tts: Then came the change. Between about two point four and two point one billion years ago, oxygen rose, wavered, and finally stayed. In bathtub terms, more was now arriving than the drains could take. Why the balance tipped then is still debated. Geologists call this the Great Oxygenation Event.
scenes.caption: Then came the change. Between about 2.4 and 2.1 billion years ago, oxygen rose, wavered, and finally stayed. In bathtub terms, more was now arriving than the drains could take. Why the balance tipped then is still debated. Geologists call this the Great Oxygenation Event.
scenes.visual: On 'the change': the band on the scrubber lights BLUE; its edges sit at the computed positions for 2.4 and 2.1 on the linear scale, and the readout reads 'about 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago'. The playhead moves through the band during the sentence. On 'oxygen rose': blue pips that break the surface now stay; the sky begins to collect them and the gauge climbs. On 'wavered': the gauge drops back, climbs, drops a little, and the pips wink out and return. On 'finally stayed': the gauge settles at a low, steady level, far below the 'today' tick, and about five pips drift in the sky for good; the tag under the gauge changes to 'schematic; levels uncertain'. On 'bathtub terms': the words 'tap' and 'drains' and the tag 'analogy' return for this one sentence; the gauge tube pulses as the tub's level; on 'drains could take' one bubble is followed past every drain tick and out through the surface, where it stays as a pip. On 'Great Oxygenation Event': 'tap', 'drains' and 'analogy' fade and that name writes on in BLUE, size 34, across the top of the sky. Animator: draw no cause. The sentence is bookkeeping, not a reason. Do not thin the iron, shrink the plume or grow the mat in this scene; the takers keep taking; the picture shows only the outcome, that some bubbles now get through and stay.
scenes.narration: Then came the change. Between about 2.4 and 2.1 billion years ago, oxygen rose, wavered, and finally stayed. In bathtub terms, more was now arriving than the drains could take. Why the balance tipped then is still debated. Geologists call this the Great Oxygenation Event.

scenes.tts: But the tub was nowhere near full. Oxygen stayed far below today's level for a very long time.
scenes.visual: The event name shrinks to a small tag on the scrubber band. The sky stays dark (it does not turn blue: sky colour is not the oxygen); the five pips drift. On 'nowhere near full': the view moves to the gauge; a white double-headed arrow opens between the low steady level and the dashed 'today' tick. On 'far below': the tag 'far below today' lands on the arrow. On 'a very long time': the playhead creeps on to the right, well past the band, and the readout reads 'later' (no number); the gauge level trembles but the arrow does not close; one pip is taken by the plume and another arrives from the sea, so the count stays at about five. Mat, flakes, plume and purple cells all keep moving.
scenes.narration: But the tub was nowhere near full. Oxygen stayed far below today's level for a very long time.

scenes.tts: Now remember the old microbes. An oxygen molecule that is only partly filled with electrons can damage D N A and proteins. For many of those microbes, oxygen was toxic. So what happened to them? Was there a mass die-off?
scenes.caption: Now remember the old microbes. An oxygen molecule that is only partly filled with electrons can damage DNA and proteins. For many of those microbes, oxygen was toxic. So what happened to them? Was there a mass die-off?
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole world after the event: five pips in the sky, gauge low and steady, the striped stack, the mat streaming. On 'old microbes': the view sinks to the seabed and the bookmark tick from s03 flares on its cluster of PURPLE cells. Then push in on the shelf near the mat until ONE purple cell is large: a rounded PURPLE outline holding two plain chips, 'DNA' and 'protein' (labelled boxes, no structures). A HERO BUBBLE drifts in beside it, already holding one YELLOW dot in one of its four sockets; three sockets are empty. It settles before the narrator says 'partly filled'; on those words the three empty sockets pulse and the bubble turns jagged and flickers. On 'can damage': the bubble brushes the cell and the two chips crack and dim. (Four things on screen: bubble, cell, two chips.) On 'was toxic': pull back to the shelf; blue bubbles drift toward the purple cells nearest the mat and those cells shrink back from them. On 'what happened': the question writes on, size 34: 'What happened to the old microbes?' On 'mass die': a second line lands under it, the tempting answer: 'A mass die-off?'
scenes.narration: Now remember the old microbes. An oxygen molecule that is only partly filled with electrons can damage DNA and proteins. For many of those microbes, oxygen was toxic. So what happened to them? Was there a mass die-off?

scenes.visual: Hold the question. Both lines stay. Bubbles keep drifting toward the purple cells on the shelf and the cells keep flinching; the purple cells on the basin floor and in the mud keep wobbling as before; flakes fall; the surface shimmers. No die-off is shown; at most one or two cells nearest the mat dim.

scenes.tts: A mass die-off is often claimed, but the evidence is thin. Microbes that live without oxygen are called anaerobes. They clearly survived, in mud, deep water and other airless places. They thrive there still, including in your own gut.
scenes.visual: The first line of the question fades and 'A mass die-off?' stays alone. On 'evidence is thin': those words go hollow (outline only) and thin away to nothing. On 'live without oxygen': the view drops below the shelf and the basin floor: the mud layer and the deep basin water are dark and free of blue bubbles, and they are full of busy PURPLE cells; on the shelf, the few purple cells nearest the mat dim and fade while those already in the mud and deep water carry on. On 'called anaerobes': the label 'anaerobes' (old-life purple, size 30) lands among them, after they have been seen. On 'clearly survived': the cells in the dark pulse and some split in two; labels land as named: 'mud', 'deep water'. On 'thrive there still': the playhead stays where it is and a small round inset opens at lower right, a plain dark tube cross-section packed with the same wobbling purple cells, label 'your gut, today' (the label carries the date).
scenes.narration: A mass die-off is often claimed, but the evidence is thin. Microbes that live without oxygen are called anaerobes. They clearly survived, in mud, deep water and other airless places. They thrive there still, including in your own gut.

scenes.tts: The oxygen that was left over did not end the old world of life. It pushed it into the shadows.
scenes.visual: The gut inset stays open for the first words, then closes. On 'left over': pull back to the whole world; the blue is where it has been allowed to stay (bubbles in the shallows, five pips in the sky), and none of it is in the mud or the deep basin. On 'did not end': the purple cells in the mud and the deep basin brighten. On 'into the shadows': a soft dark band settles over mud and deep basin and the purple cells glow inside it, while pips drift in the sky above; the frame is now two worlds stacked, lit above and dark below. The bookmark tick from s03 sits inside the dark band, on a living cluster.
scenes.narration: The oxygen that was left over did not end the old world of life. It pushed it into the shadows.

scenes.tts: Now run the clock forward. Oxygen stayed low for well over a billion years. Then, much later, it rose again, toward the level you breathe today. Take that breath again. It began as waste. And what reaches your lungs is what the rest of the planet left behind.
scenes.visual: On 'forward to today': the playhead runs to the right end, 'today'; as it runs there, the grey dissolved-iron discs fade out of the sea and the red flakes stop falling; the striped stack stays on the floor as finished rock; the gauge fill cross-fades (no sweep, no drawn path: the script gives none) up to the dashed 'today' tick and the sky fills with drifting BLUE pips, as in the first shot. No plant, leaf or green land is drawn: the script does not say where today's oxygen makers came from. On 'that breath again': the view rises into the sky to the opening framing, pips drifting toward the viewer. On 'began as waste': one pip is traced by a thin blue line back down to the vent of the mat. On 'left behind': the view pulls back one last time to the whole world, and the pip trail is shown slipping past the takers still at work, the plume and the shore, and over the red striped stack, the record of what the sea once took. The purple cells still glow in the dark band. Sea surface, plume, mat, pips and purple cells keep moving; there are no iron discs and no falling flakes. REVISED 2026-11-09: the gauge holds low while the playhead runs on (label 'low for over a billion years'), then climbs in a second step to 'today' on 'rose again'.
scenes.narration: Now run the clock forward. Oxygen stayed low for well over a billion years. Then, much later, it rose again, toward the level you breathe today. Take that breath again. It began as waste. And what reaches your lungs is what the rest of the planet left behind.

scenes.visual: End card over the dimmed, still-moving world as it stands at 'today' (no iron discs, no falling flakes; the striped stack on the floor): 'The air keeps only the oxygen that nothing else takes first.' with biochemistrypedia.com beneath. Never the title.
